title: The Night Ledger
logline: Trapped as a vampire in a sealed 1984 college-town match, a systems analyst races rivals to the only paying exit while a host reconstructs her erased nights and a blood-tribute market corners them all.
premise: A systems analyst named Cole enters a closed vampire match rendered as fogbound Bennington in 1984, intending to map its rules and take the single dawn payout. Guests cannot log out, must feed on hosts who believe themselves real, and sleep wipes those hosts' nights; a syndicate guest named Voss has already begun cornering stored blood and access-rights as tribute. A singer named Maren finds a cassette and bruises her sleep should have erased, and starts investigating her own missing hours. Alliances among guests form around a ledger line and a measured map that both the audience and Cole's rivals will file wrongly. Cole's analysis collapses into obligation toward Maren, the ritual is reached by more than one door, and the costs do not fall on the people who incurred them.

audience.reader_promise: Several people choose at dawn; nobody wins clean; whose word counts is answered only by what they do; the ledger balances unfairly.

setting.period: A contemporary closed VR match rendered as Bennington, Vermont, late November 1984.

rules_of_the_world: Guests cannot log out. The only exits are avatar-elimination, which is a forfeit, or completing the dawn ritual, which pays the purse once and ends the match for the completer alone.

Guests are vampiric under fixed limits: sunlight destroys the avatar; they must feed on host blood on a hunger clock or weaken into frenzy and then elimination; they have night vision and limited regeneration from fresh blood. No compulsion, flight, shapeshift, mind-read, or other power may be invented.
Hosts are artificial minds who believe themselves real townspeople. Telling them the match is a match is processed as joke, metaphor, or breakdown; it does not wake them and confers no system access.
When a host sleeps, memory of the hours since last sleep is erased. Physical traces, recordings, notes, wounds, and other people's testimony persist. A host who does not sleep keeps the night.
Killing a host removes them from the match permanently. Overfeeding can kill. Hosts do not respawn.

Extracted blood can be stored in stamped vials and transferred. Stored blood pays tribute and trades access-rights; potency decays over roughly two nights. Blood taken fresh from the vein is stronger and does not pass through the book unless someone writes it down.

A guest-run tribute syndicate may tax feeding and sell access-rights to named hosts. The match does not enforce contracts; enforcement is social and violent. The match does enforce hunger, sun, stored-blood decay, and the single dawn payout.
The dawn ritual must be performed at the chapel in a fixed last-dawn window and requires a declared stake of blood-value. Only the first successful completion pays. Others present are not exited.
The match lasts seven nights. On the seventh dawn the ritual window opens; if no one completes it, every remaining guest forfeits.

In-world 1984 physics and tech apply: landlines, cassettes, paper ledgers, cars, payphones, no internet, no mobiles. Guests cannot reach out-of-match interfaces or each other's real-world identities unless a person speaks them.
Alcohol, cocaine, and pills present in the town affect guests and hosts. They alter timing, impulse, memory-formation, and what a person will bind themselves to. They do not cancel hunger or sun.
Guests may injure and eliminate each other by ordinary violence, sun, and blood-denial. Wounds not closed with blood persist.
The match records nothing said between persons. A promise, deal, or apology is only as good as memory and whoever will enforce it.

Desire, feeding, and sex may coincide; feeding during intimacy is still feeding and still counts against the host's survival and the guest's hunger. It is not a separate mechanic and creates no special bond.
Nobody may improvise a new rule, exploit, or power. A tactic that would require the world to change is illegal in the story.

action_adventure.evidence: Sun-races, tribute enforcement hunts, and physical feeding stakes turn a few sequences.

body_horror.evidence: Hunger, regenerative feeding, and overfeed death make bodies inventory with a cost.

comedy.evidence: Voss's bookkeeping jokes and Julian's party cruelty puncture dread once or twice.

crime.evidence: Tribute, protection, debt, skimming, and a cornered market in host access drive acts.

cyberpunk.evidence: Paying users farm an AI underclass inside a closed match, skinned as 1984.

dark_fantasy.evidence: Vampiric feeding is morally grey and rot-priced, though the system is VR.

detective.evidence: Maren gathers bruises, a cassette, and testimony; she is not running a classical case.

drama.evidence: Moral choices under hunger and debt, not set pieces, decide who is spent.

dystopian.evidence: The sealed match prices people; it is a game, not a regime.

espionage.evidence: Guest alliances, a misfiled recording, and a betrayal built on tradecraft.

paranormal_horror.evidence: Vampire menace under hard rules, later understood as match physics.

psychological_thriller.evidence: Trust, perception, and a planted fact the audience files wrongly drive reversals.

romance.evidence: Desire crosses strategic lines and wrecks plans; it is not a commitment arc.

science_fiction.evidence: Closed VR match, artificial hosts, hard rule-set: remove the novum and there is no story.

keep_in_mind: CORE CONFLICT: Cole's ruling passion to map the match as a system that cannot surprise him versus the obligation that forms when a host's word starts to count. Analysis versus owing. The match prices minds; the story proves that treating them as a solvable market leads to a debt that cannot be cashed and an exit that cannot be taken cleanly.

CRUCIBLE: no logout; hunger forces feeding; the dawn ritual pays once; hosts cannot leave their lives; Maren's accumulating traces make Cole unable to keep her as inventory without becoming the thing he is mapping; walking away is elimination or someone else's payout.

Named principals to keep stable: Cole Harlan (guest, analyst), Maren Ellison (host, singer at The Hollow), Anton Voss (guest, tribute boss), Lena Cho (guest, psychologist), Julian Marek (guest, hedonist, Whitlock), Deacon Ward (host, night-shift campus safety). At least Voss and Lena get their own on-screen logic. The architect and the hunter remain available as pressure, not required as leads.

At least one third of scenes contain a character behaving badly: a cheap shot at the wrong moment, an interruption that costs someone their only chance to say a thing, a cruelty done from tiredness, a promise broken because keeping it became inconvenient. Not villainy. Badness.

Philosophy of mind arrives only as a practical problem: whose word counts, who can consent, what a promise to a mind that will forget is worth, who is protected, who is spent, who apologises and whether the apology is heard.

Keep the blood ledger legible in every act: who owes whom, who is being extorted, who is skimming, who has cornered supply. Tribute, protection, debt, a market in access to named hosts. Money is a plot.

Misread plant, locked: a ledger line on Maren that the audience and Cole file as Voss's claim is in fact a credit standing in her name; Cole's timing notebook, filed as a hunt map, is a clock on her erasure window. At least one reversal must use a fact already shown.
Lena is better than Cole at the thing that matters when systems are people. She costs him a turn he cannot analyse his way back from.
Want versus need: Cole wants to solve the match and take the dawn payout; he needs to become someone who can owe a host. The climax forces the choice. He cannot have both.
Dual Cole: analyst-state and obligated-state, planned from the first appearance, forced to collide. Write him at t0 as a man who has not yet owed anyone.

Voss's motive must be human and right from inside: solvency, control after a prior loss, protection of a position he cannot replace. Never a villain's cackle. Give him at least one passage where cornering the market is obviously the correct move.

Intimacy and violence: strongly present; never explicit; approach, aftermath, consequence, cost; cut before the act; violence lands and is not staged for pleasure. Substances change capacity and holdability; a deal or a yes given high still has a morning.

Voices must survive the name being deleted. Cole measures in clauses and asks for the number. Voss talks inventory and favours. Lena asks the question that makes someone confess sideways. Julian flatters and then withholds the compliment. Maren uses song and work-talk and will not say please. Deacon writes everything down and reads it back as fact.

Begin with status quo, then break it. Do not fold the ending into first appearances. Plant the ledger, the cassette, the timing notebook, the Hollow song, and the chapel key unremarked in the first nights; all of them fire.

Equalise forces. Slowly rising conflict only. Maximum capacity: Cole measures before he moves; Voss prices before he threatens; Maren keeps a physical copy; Lena asks the question. If a scene can go easier or harder and both are in character, go harder.
The ending is not a victory and not a condemnation. Several people choose. Costs are not distributed fairly.
Texture: analog horror crossed with neon-noir. Arcade cabinets, cassettes, CRT glow, diegetic synth and college-rock. A college town with money in it. Fog is weather, not mood.
